newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis feel Rabin's loss a year on.
newsitem.headline: Israelis feel Rabin's loss a year on.

text.p: As Israelis grapple with the Palestinian peace deal that is Yitzhak Rabin's legacy and face fresh tensions with Arab neighbours, they say they miss the man who was nicknamed "Mr Security".

A year after a right-wing Jewish gunman killed the Israeli prime minister, the news is dominated by disputes with the Palestinians on the ground and at the negotiating table and by a threat of war with Syria.
Despite deep divisions among Israelis, an opinion poll for the newspaper Maariv in mid-October showed 79 percent felt Rabin's absence to the Jewish state.
"You're missed, friend" said hundreds of thousands of bumper stickers that Israel's best-selling daily Yedioth Ahronoth issued with its last big weekend edition.
Gruff but shy, the ruddy-faced native-born former general personified what Israelis still say they felt when he reluctantly shook the hand of long-shunned PLO head Yasser Arafat.
"The awkwardness of the handshake reflected the ambivalence Israelis felt about Arafat and the profound lack of trust that existed and still exists," said Jerusalem philosopher Rabbi David Hartman.
"He (Rabin) had the strength to overcome those self-doubts and move the country to a new plateau," Hartman said.

When in 1993 Rabin sealed a landmark accord with the Palestinians, defending it as a calculated risk for peace, critics accused him of breaking every important promise he ever made. Some branded him a traitor.
Gunman Yigal Amir killed him for it after a Tel Aviv peace rally on November 4, 1995.
Israelis however followed Rabin because, perhaps more than anyone, they trusted him with their security.
"He was a big brother who was always there for them, protecting them," said Uri Dromi, who was Rabin's spokesman.
As chief of staff during the 1967 Middle East war Rabin led Israel to a decisive victory, capturing the West Bank, Sinai, Golan and Gaza in six days from Jordan, Egypt and Syria.

After a 27-year army career, Rabin entered politics, reminding Israelis of his military credentials with iron-fisted responses to Arab-Israeli violence that included ordering soldiers to break Palestinian bones and, once, expelling 415 Palestinians to Lebanon.

"As long as Yitzhak Rabin was there, even when not at the top, even at times when he was in opposition or only the minister of defence, people knew that when they slept, someone was awake worrying about their security," Dromi said.
The thinking went: If Yitzhak Rabin could make concessions for peace, who were other Israelis to say no?
Many right-wingers saw it differently, vilifying Rabin at rallies against his peace deals. At one demonstration, a protester carried a poster depicting him in a Nazi SS uniform.

Asked to define Rabin's legacy, Shimon Peres, his Labour party partner, told Reuters last week it was that the two of them, men in their 70s, had taken the tough decisions on peace that would have been unfair to leave to a younger generation.

When last May, Likud right-winger Benjamin Netanyahu ousted Peres by fewer than 30,000 votes, it was because voters perceived Netanyahu would ensure a safer Israel. A perpetual loser in Israeli elections, Peres without Rabin was not Rabin.
Many expect Netanyahu will follow in the slain leader's footsteps, perhaps at a slower pace, having no choice but to carry out the deals Rabin left him.
They believe Netanyahu, having won over the Israeli centre by promising "peace and security", will have to deliver both if he has any hope of being re-elected in the year 2000.
"You don't see that they've come up with a totally new idea or formula. It's still the Palestinians who are our partners. Arafat is still the main partner," Dromi said.

"I watched Netanyahu shaking his (Arafat's) hand. The fact is that here is the prime minister of Israel grabbing the hand of Arafat and shaking it with both hands -- that's more than Rabin did when he first shook the hand."

If and when the Palestinian problem is resolved, Rabin may be remembered as the Israeli leader who had the wisdom, the courage -- and the security credentials -- to accomplish what he called the toppling of psychological barriers.
